title: 🌿 Eryndor Living Culture Atlas IX — Smaller Peoples & Regional Traditions
rawNotionMarkup: Eryndor Living Culture Atlas IX — smaller, scattered and unconventional peoples. Complements Atlas VIII and covers Halflings, Gnomes, Goblins, Ents, Centaurs, Merfolk, Giants, Kobolds, Satyrs/Fauns, Pixies, Minotaurs, Brownies/Boggarts, Ogres, Trolls, Mushroom folk and Harpies, plus the exceptional Living Mountains. Every entry contains several distinct subcultures, not one species-wide behavior. Proposed group names, rituals and civic institutions are new/revisable; original established species remain untouched. No birth-rate changes, fertility assumptions or compulsory household size. Species ≠ culture ≠ individual morality. ## Western Avarra species-frequency clarification — Goblins specifically (21 November 2026) Latest creator correction: Goblins, specifically, are commonplace throughout the expanded western continent, roaming roads and countryside in travelling groups while also maintaining longstanding permanent villages, trade towns, guild quarters and mixed communities. Do not interpret 'roam' as nomadic-only. This should be visible in rural demographics, markets, road encounters, cultural geography and new private Khazari cartography. Ogres are still an established intelligent people with their own settlements and individual lives, but the creator's correction does not establish that Ogres are equally widespread or numerous across the west. Their prevalence and specific home territories remain subject to later decisions. Earlier prose that paired 'Goblins and Ogres' as equally commonplace across western Avarra is superseded as to Ogre prevalence. No demographic inflation: This distributes existing Avarran Goblin numbers within the established sixfold model rather than creating additional people. Retain the eastern/southeastern badlands Urakai creative direction and no settled Urakai eastern grassland communities as previously clarified; do not create a new Ogre/Goblin kingdom, named settlement, ruler or campaign event just from a frequency preference. ## All established peoples in western Avarra and the Urakai southeastern badlands — creator reminder (21 November 2026) Do not omit the eccentric/small/large folk: The creator specifically requires the expanded Avarran west and the Urakai-inhabited badlands to include appropriate communities of the other already-established peoples, including Ogres and whimsical or fairy-tale-feeling peoples. These are full intelligent peoples with family, political agency, economies, differing customs and serious as well as funny lives, not props, servants or uniformly comedic species. This complements the earlier requirement for multiple Eldar and Aelwyn elder communities, two human culture belts, Gnome/Pixie settlements, and Urakai cities in the southeastern wastes. No previously counted population is being added twice. Existing peoples to preserve across the wider atlas: Khazari, Eldar, Urakai, Humans, Halflings, Gnomes, Goblins, Ents, Centaurs, Merfolk, Giants, Wolvenkin, Foxfolk, Lionfolk, Tigerfolk, Elephantfolk, Bearfolk, Cowfolk, Pigfolk, Kobolds, Satyrs/Fauns, Pixies, Minotaurs, Brownies/Boggarts, Ogres, Trolls, Mushroom folk, Harpies; also rare/unquantified Drakari, Aelwyn Fae and Living Mountains. Do not conflate Aelwyn Fae with Pixies or Brownies; do not invent Mousefolk or import named fairy-tale characters without an explicit creator decision. No species is inherently good or evil because its look is fanciful. Proposed placement ecology and everyday life—not a fixed monopoly or new sovereign roster: - Giant expanded Letharion and western old-growth: Eldar courts, Ent grove federations, Aelwyn seasonal enclaves, Pixie canopy villages, Satyr/Faun orchards, Brownie/Boggart hedge/household boroughs, Mushroom-folk damp wood settlements, woodland Goblin and Gnome quarters, forest-friendly Troll households, and mixed hamlets with Halflings, Foxfolk and others. Protected and sparsely traveled sacred stretches remain between settled cores. - Western agrarian plains, river towns and temperate wetlands: Halfling farmers, Pigfolk bakers/millers, Cowfolk dairies, Foxfolk couriers/merchants, Gnome waterworks, Kobold brick/drainage guilds, Goblin markets, human river and estate cultures, Satyr orchards, river-loving Trolls and practical Ogre quarry/road/transport workers. Ogres may instead own businesses, hold offices, farm, study or simply live family lives; roles are options, not biological restrictions. - Far-west storm coast, western highlands, peninsulas and islands: Distinct human maritime culture, Wolvenkin and Bearfolk communities, Goblin and Gnome docks, Ogre and Giant upland settlements, Harpy cliff-side towns and courier routes, coastal Merfolk polities with negotiated shore access; perhaps Centaur grassland hinterlands and mixed Minotaur communities. Remote Drakari and Living Mountain possibilities remain unlocated and unquantified; their actual territories are not decided by illustrative dots. - Urakai southeastern badlands and wastes: Permanent Urakai canyon/well/volcanic-upland cities and tribal confederations, interspersed with Ogre families/clans and settlements, cave-and-quarry Goblins, Kobolds and Gnomes, Troll enclaves around springs/stone ravines, caravan-oriented Minotaurs and Centaurs along viable grazing fringes, small Harpy cliff settlements, and individual/mixed communities of Lionfolk, Tigerfolk, Elephantfolk, Pigfolk, Foxfolk and humans wherever ecological and trade conditions allow. Arid regions require water, food, storage, routes, trade and craftsmanship. Do not imply all Ogres, Trolls or Goblins live in the wastes or are vassals of one Urakai monarch. Uninhabitable expanses remain genuinely empty. Map implementation: On a large private Khazari chart of Avarra show major established kingdoms and all seven correctly placed Throne cities around the Ironspine-encircled Veiled Inland Sea; leave a vast thousands-of-miles west; label enormous northern/western Letharion Forest, northwest coldlands, west rural plains and far-west port cultures, the southwestern Shattered Gulf, southern open country/Crown Sea and massive eastern/southeastern Urakai-populated wastes and badlands. Depict mixed-species villages, little forest boroughs, caravan cities and Ogre/Troll communities using subtle settlement glyphs or small illustrated vignettes without overwhelming broad geography. Inner-basin villages connect to each other by shore roads and ferries, but public outsiders lack ordinary passage. Do not invent or canonize new government names, exact census values, moon counts, dates or map scale bars from generated art; no character knowledge or campaign event changes. Demographic protection: Reuse the creator-adopted 6× modeled populations (Avarra 1,019.760m; world 2,062.800m), allocating already-existing continent and species totals into regionally plausible habitats rather than adding populations. Aelwyn and exceptional rare peoples still lack precise numeric censuses; existing birth rates and cultural diversity are unchanged. ## Era of Fire — third and final era of the Second Age, 116 years (creator canon, 21 November 2026) AVARRAN HISTORICAL NAME, CREATOR-ESTABLISHED: The third and final Avarran-defined era of Eryndor's Second Age is called the Era of Fire; other continents may name or divide the period differently. It lasted 116 years, corresponding to Second Age Years 1,322–1,437 inclusive. Its exact duration is derived from the already confirmed Second Age total: 1,437 − 321 years (Era of Awakening) − 1,000 years (Era of Wonder) = 116 years. Chronology: (1) Era of Awakening, Years 1–321, 321 years; (2) Era of Wonder, Years 322–1,321, 1,000 years; (3) Era of Fire, Years 1,322–1,437, 116 years. The catastrophic global earthquakes at the end of the Era of Fire ended the Second Age and began the Third Age. Their causes, seismic effects, sudden marshland and lowland mountain uplift, tenfold global aftershock amplification through the ancient Ironspine, mass deaths without whole-species extinction and the as-yet-undefined magical protection are recorded separately, not invented here. STRICTLY UNWRITTEN INTERIOR OF ERA: The creator explicitly requested no new racial, cultural, political, military, magical, religious or event history be filled into this third era yet. Only its name, length, place in the chronology and already creator-approved ending catastrophe are established. “Fire” has no confirmed source or metaphorical meaning; do not assume volcanoes, wars, dragons, burning moons, fire magic, apocalyptic conflagration, Fire Gods, or any particular ruler, kingdom, people or First Throne connection. The open First Throne storyline remains genuinely unselected; Gloin's ancestry and campaign scene remain unaffected. ## Urakai / Orcs — FIRST APPEAR IN THE THIRD AGE, absent from First and Second Ages (binding creator correction, 21 November 2026) CANON CHRONOLOGICAL RULE — supersedes conflicting earlier text: Urakai (Orcs) did not exist in the First Age or anywhere in the 1,437-year Second Age. The exiled dark mages of southeastern Avarra created the Orcs sometime during the Third Age. The exact Third Age year, creation method, first location, identities of the first communities, and subsequent structure of mage–Orc command remain UNDECIDED. The Orcs were absent from the Second Age's Era of Awakening (Years 1–321), Era of Wonder (Years 322–1,321) and Era of Fire (Years 1,322–1,437). Earlier lore depicting Orc inhabitants, clans, armies, cities or events in either of those two Ages is superseded and noncanon. Goblins and Ogres may predate the Third Age. CREATOR CANON — Third Age creation and intended conquests: The exiled dark mages who formed the southeastern Avarran Southern Wastes and its volcano during the Second Age survived well into the Third Age, when they created the Urakai (Orcs) by a method not yet decided. Their ambition in creating the Orcs was first to besiege the dwarven (Khazari) strongholds, and ultimately to attack the Eldar and human kingdoms. This establishes the mages' intentions, not any particular siege, conquest, campaign, chronology, victory or attack as an accomplished fact. The mages established no diplomacy, trade, treaties or alliances with pre-existing outside peoples; creating the Orcs is an act of creation for the mages' ambitions, not evidence of diplomatic relations. The exact magical or other creation process, timing, first Orc settlements, degree and duration of mage control, and later independence or resistance remain open. The modern Urakai are a diverse people with their own cultures and agency; they are not collectively evil, personally culpable for the mages' acts, or necessarily still subject to their creators. Effects on war histories: Any established older east–west wars involving Urakai, and any historical Goblin/Ogre alliances or assistance with Orc forces, must have happened in the Third Age or later, with no specific Age within that range, reign, battle, migration date or formal state assigned yet. The anti-Goblin, anti-Ogre and anti-Urakai prejudices of western Avarra remain valid consequences of those undated wars. These cannot predate the Third Age. Nor should living Urakai's settled southeast badlands homelands and their modern peoples/cultures be erased or treated as magically evil due to a speculative ancient link. Canon controls and campaign: Modern Urakai exist in large numbers, with sophisticated diverse societies, independent cities, families, economies, politics, culture and varied morality. Existing Fifth Age maps and sixfold census are unchanged; this corrects only their ancestral chronology. No changes to family rates, species lifespans or present demographics. The no-species-extinction rule at the Second Age-ending earthquake stays: Urakai were not a species that survived that disaster, because they had not appeared yet; all peoples existing at that time survived somewhere. Do not connect their origin to Gloin Hammerfeld's genuinely unknown genealogy, the First Throne, the lost First Age moon-magics or the yet-unexplained global species-survival magical force without an explicit new creator decision. ## Second Age racial histories II — other established and fairy-tale peoples (Awakening and Wonder ONLY, creator-authorized expansion, 21 November 2026) STATUS: Established historical patterns added under creator authority for the Era of Awakening (Second Age Years 1–321) and Era of Wonder (Years 322–1,321) only. These are shared strands, not mandatory personalities, claims of a single original homeland, newly created species, founding dates for modern cities, or official histories of the Era of Fire. ### Halflings — the continuity of a hearth - Awakening: Kin networks and neighborhood ovens preserved seed, food, medicine, children's teaching and the memory of dependable nonmagical methods after food-preserving enchantments faltered. Some made generous refuge houses, others protected only their families; homeliness was no universal law. - Wonder: Small-scale lunar protections, gardencraft and practical household magic became studied arts alongside farming, navigation and trade. Halfling merchants carried techniques between settlements; others became bold healers, travelers or skeptical craft teachers. A good harvest was celebrated as the joint labor of soil, people and magic, not proof that a moon would always provide. ### Gnomes — the first honest experiments - Awakening: Gnomish experimenters established repeatable nonmagical tests to distinguish failed materials from altered lunar responses. A useful custom, the Empty Bench, required apprentices to attempt a device's function without enchantment before proposing a magical improvement. It was practiced by some schools rather than decreed by all Gnomes. - Wonder: New lunar disciplines inspired miniature observatories, clever mechanical safeguards, traveling experiment caravans and playful public demonstrations. Gnomish schools competed over safety versus speed, with risky failures sometimes causing suffering. This does not establish the existence or date of the still-mysterious ancient 'Impossible Engine'. ### Goblins — keeping what the catastrophe could not take - Awakening: Goblin households, traders and small cooperative settlements learned to conserve fuel, salvage usable tools, share hidden routes and protect food when enchanted stores failed. Some were generous allies, others profiteered or raided, and many groups mistrusted powerful outsiders who wanted their supplies. These events did NOT establish the later eastern–western alliance wars or modern stereotypes. - Wonder: Some Goblin communities became celebrated for exacting enchantment appraisals, compact craftsmanship, lively markets and mutual-aid credit. Careful bargaining and independent testing helped merchants navigate unfamiliar new magics; schools of lockwork and magical concealment developed in different places. The common later accusation that all Goblins are thieves remains prejudice, not an ancient truth. ### Ents — remembering the living ground - Awakening: Ancient forest stewards responded to inconsistent lunar light by relying on the World's Breath and the resilience of roots, watersheds and living soil. Some moved to shield younger groves, while others argued that interference with settlements would worsen the damage. Their deliberations could be infuriatingly slow to short-lived neighbors. - Wonder: Ent circles cooperated with diverse forest peoples in techniques that respected ecological limits while incorporating newly mastered moon-derived effects. They preserved living memory and protected ancient groves, but no Ent was granted an infallible pre-Cataclysm archival record. Their councils were not uniformly benevolent or politically united. ### Centaurs — paths written without enchantment - Awakening: Centaur communities re-established water sources, seasonal trails and safe movement across open land as magical direction-finding became uncertain. Pasture rights, mutual rescue and disagreement over settled versus wandering lives shaped their households. - Wonder: New moon-born weather observations, healing arts and travel wards enriched communities on grassland, steppe and frontier. Some worked with road engineers or urban scholars while others defended mobile autonomy. No single world-spanning Centaur confederacy or Urakai treaty was founded by this account. ### Merfolk — sounding the changed tides - Awakening: Coastal and inland-water Merfolk charted unfamiliar lunar effects on currents and magical navigation while using direct soundings, dive marks, trained observers and cooperative rescues. Sea and freshwater societies differed, and the collapse of a particular spell could have different consequences in a reef than a river delta. - Wonder: Academies of tide observation, current-craft and enchanted signaling developed in separate underwater polities. Exchanges with surface shipwrights and river traders encouraged prosperous mixed maritime networks. These arts did not require a named patron moon or establish a uniform Merfolk kingdom. ### Giants — the weight of practical shelter - Awakening: Giants in highlands and coldlands improved large-scale bridges, shelter stones and storage through direct labor when runic weatherworks or protections failed. Some rescued smaller peoples, some demanded payment and some took what they wanted. The scale of their work never implied a single culture. - Wonder: Giant masons and sky observers combined surviving skills with new lunar arts for safe high-altitude travel, enormous construction and ritual oratory. Their schools could be fiercely independent of smaller states. No connection to the sentient Living Mountains is defined. ### Kobolds — the measure of a safe tunnel - Awakening: Colony and household builders learned to distrust untested enchanted supports and establish physically marked escape routes, ventilated chambers and reliable communal stores. Arguments over whether to reopen damaged galleries became part of practical civic life. - Wonder: Kobold miners, artisans and careful underground architects mastered compact magical ventilation, ore testing and intricate lightworks while keeping manual backup systems. Mixed-species settlements bought their expertise; other Kobolds pursued scholarship, farming or music instead of tunnelcraft. ### Satyrs and Fauns — joy after uncertainty - Awakening: Woodland and meadow societies kept nonmagical song, dance and communal hospitality alive where magical festivities had become perilous. Some communities offered safe refuges, while others withdrew or fiercely defended scarce grazing and orchard lands. - Wonder: New lunar magics enriched living performance, festivals, sympathetic garden rituals and peaceful intercommunity exchange. Yet some celebrants saw indulgence as an abuse of power, and others preferred strict stewardship. Music was a chosen art, not the compulsory nature of every Satyr or Faun. ### Pixies — small shelters, intricate miracles - Awakening: Winged families suffered disproportionately when tiny enchanted dwellings and flight wards became unsafe; they built physical windbreaks, shelter networks and systems for warning larger neighbors about unnoticed dangers. They did not all become harmless pranksters or helpless victims. - Wonder: Fine lunar craft enriched delicate architecture, messenger systems, miniature healing tools and concealed gardens. Some Pixie towns developed strict safety laws around enchantment, while travelling performers used new powers flamboyantly. Their hidden villages and populous neighborhoods were genuine societies, not decorative folklore. ### Minotaurs — more than the walls around them - Awakening: Minotaur communities mapped evacuation routes, reinforced gathering halls and supplied heavy labor when magically guided passages became deceptive. Some developed a practical ethic of honest directions; others guarded private refuges or exploited the vulnerable. - Wonder: Diverse Minotaur architects, philosophers, navigators and fighters studied spatial enchantments and newly magical construction, blending them with nonmagical design. Those in wide savannas pursued entirely different priorities from citizens of dense cities. No universal labyrinth cult or Minotaur kingdom is established. ### Brownies and Boggarts — the right to be more than a household spell - Awakening: Small communities maintained shelters, chimneys, wells and stored food when domestic protections failed. Reciprocal help created lasting stories, but some powerful householders exploited these workers, and some Brownie or Boggart groups responded with mischief, resistance or withdrawal. - Wonder: Skilled home enchantments, miniature craft guilds and neighborhood warning systems grew with new lunar knowledge. Some groups lived visibly in towns, others kept their doors hidden. Their relationship as biological lineages or cultural labels remains unknown; no obligation to serve other peoples is implied. ### Ogres — from swamp hearths to great public works - Awakening: Ogre families in marshes, woodland huts, islands, highlands and mixed settlements carried supplies, built robust crossings and sheltered endangered kin, while some predatory bands became objects of real fear. An isolated cauldron-lit swamp cottage and an entire organized Ogre village could both survive by practical strength and local knowledge. - Wonder: Ogre masons, healers, ferry-keepers and scholars participated in renewed magic, developing durable enchanted causeways and safe heavy transport beside the simpler charms of private huts. Swamp-island villages, cosmopolitan neighborhoods and solitary dwellers all remained valid social forms. This history does not date later alliances with Urakai or imply all Ogres are dangerous. ### Trolls — stone in moving water - Awakening: Troll communities built and guarded tangible crossings, flood retreats and winter shelters as enchantments failed. Some levied fair passage fees, others preyed upon travelers, and different cultures argued over responsibilities to outsiders. - Wonder: New spellwork enriched bridgecraft, drainage, river sensing, cliff gardens and public protections while practical engineering persisted. Troll courts and independent households made incompatible political choices. No universal regeneration, sun vulnerability or shared Troll kingdom is introduced. ### Mushroom folk — the quiet science of decay and renewal - Awakening: Mushroom folk investigated changes in soil, subterranean moisture, rot, nutrients and the independent World's Breath, learning which life processes continued without dependable lunar enchantment. Communities developed careful food preservation, sanitation and shared alerts without becoming a single hive mind. - Wonder: New lunar magics informed fungi cultivation, dye, medicine and living ventilation in caverns, forests and wetlands. Distinct families and scientific circles differed over safe experimentation, reciprocity and land use. Their biology, lifespan and reproductive mechanics remain undetermined. ### Harpies — the signal above the storm - Awakening: Harpy households and roost towns adapted when moon-touched winds or sky wards became unreliable, using visible landmarks, manual beacon systems and cooperative warning calls across cliffs and coasts. Some were pirates or raiders, others guides, healers or protectors; not one aerial culture. - Wonder: New lunar enchantments expanded aeronautic signaling, cliff architecture, navigation and performance magic. Mixed port communities valued Harpy knowledge of winds and distant dangers, while aerial territories developed their own political disputes. ### Living Mountains — deliberately unresolved - Awakening and Wonder: The presence of rare sentient Living Mountains during these specific eras has not been firmly dated. Later peoples told stories that a mountain remembered the changing moons or spoke at a festival, but such stories are reported legends, not authenticated Second Age encounters. Their nature, numbers and connection to the ancient nonsentient Ironspine ring remain unknown; do not conflate them. Common continuity: The Era of Wonder did not revive magics whose destroyed moons ceased to exist; it mastered newer fragment-born powers, alongside viable older traditions and the planet's independent Natural Magic. Folklore residences and substantial mixed or species-majority societies coexisted, with some magically hidden. All first-two-era examples are geographically broad and do not fix modern city founding dates, eastern–western war dates, exact moons, population totals, species ancestry or Third-Era events. ## Reading the social atlas The same people can have rural, urban, elite, diasporic, regional and countercultural identities. Social ideals can be debated or weaponized. Large families, extended clan obligations, adoptive kin and childless households can occur wherever supported by already established biology; no numerical birth-rate pattern is inferred. The home of a sapient small person is not automatically a servant quarter. A terrifying reputation can be warranted for a particular violent group without condemning every member of that people. ## Halflings — household warmth is not the only virtue | Subculture | Region and admired ways of life | What can divide people | | --- | --- | --- | | Orchard Hearths | Aldermere, western Avarra and mixed Bramblebridge farms: skilled gardeners, cooks, caretakers, family hosts, cheesemakers | A wealthy household may abuse the expectation of generous hospitality; land titles disputed | | Road-Pocket Families | Avarran merchant and northern wagon routes: storytellers, messengers, itinerant cooks, wagon owners, adopters of lost travelers | Settled relations may call them unreliable; outsiders underestimate their commercial skill | | Riverbank Co-ops | Orundel and Silverflow floodplains: irrigation, council service, navigation, mutual-aid loans | Collectivists versus successful independent barge entrepreneurs | | Deep Market Halflings | Khazari mountain-market districts: provisioners, bakers, clerks, intercultural household brokers | Different food habits, access ramps and market rent politics | Family and status: Warm large households may be respected but solitary scholars and unmarried explorers need not be universally scorned. In some villages breaking hospitality is worse than becoming wealthy; elsewhere unpayable hospitality expectations bankrupt families. Not every Halfling prefers safety. ## Gnomes — exploration, not an innate engineer job | Subculture | Regional focus and respected paths | Dilemmas | | --- | --- | --- | | Brasshall Examiners | Khazari urban guild cities: verification, careful instruments, craft education | A brilliant invention that is untested may be politically contentious | | Swingspan Wanderers | Merchant Coast, Avarran caravans and Vaeloran roads: improvised gadgets, traveling repair, linguistic agility | Repairers may sell what they cannot truly service; highly inventive rivals compete | | Glasswater Observers | Sahrad towns and scholars' gardens: astronomy, optics, surveying, teaching | Elite colleges sometimes claim monopoly over publicly useful findings | | Canopy Toolwrights | Vaeloran and Letharion woodland villages: miniature mechanisms, waterwheels, harvesting gear | Forest treaties and wood-sourcing restrictions | Family and disapproval: A family of patient teachers and a lone reckless inventor can both be respected by different communities. Some guilds shame plagiarism, some care more about demonstrable usefulness than elegant design. Looking ridiculous has no mechanical success/failure rule. ## Why Goblins, Ogres and Urakai face western prejudice — older war history (21 November 2026) Creator's historical explanation: During wars between eastern and western peoples in the Third Age or later, some eastern Goblin and Ogre groups fought with or aided Urakai. Long after Goblins and Ogres moved into western lands and established ordinary, numerous communities, memory of those alliances persisted as discrimination. Western Goblins are stereotyped as thieving/conniving and widely distrusted; Ogres are widely feared, in part due to fearsome wartime reputation; rare western Urakai visitors face antipathy tied to their eastern political and military associations. These are historically inherited prejudices, not innate racial traits or proof all ancestral groups took one side. Exact dates, war names, cultures and campaigns are OPEN. The creator also raised eastern origins and the possibility that Goblins/Ogres are distinct distant biological cousins of Urakai; biological kinship is NOT established. Eastern/southeastern badlands are the main current Urakai heartlands; the Eastern Grasslands have very rare Urakai and no established Urakai settlements. Western Goblins/Ogres remain commonplace. See 03 — History & Ancient Lore for the full historical and canon-status distinction. ## Western Avarra — feared Ogres versus distrusted Goblins (creator refinement, 21 November 2026) Ogres are feared across much of western Avarra. Their size, physical power and often exaggerated reputation for violence provoke genuine apprehension: guards may be visibly tense, isolated villages nervous, innkeepers reluctant and children told frightening tales. This is a social perception, not a statement that all Ogres are violent or hostile. Ogres are common western inhabitants with their own families, villages, trades, civic lives and varied personalities. Fear may lead to exclusion or unequal treatment in some places, but no uniform kingdom-wide Ogre persecution is automatically established. Goblins are distrusted, particularly on the persistent stereotypes that they are thieving, conniving, scheming or dishonest. Those prejudices cause heavy discrimination in markets, guilds, courts, property rights and everyday dealings in many western societies. Some Goblins genuinely commit crimes, as members of any other people can; the stereotype is not an innate trait or a reliable assessment of an individual. Goblins too are common established western residents, not a universally criminal, nomadic or villainous species. Different towns, governments and individuals vary greatly in how hostile or welcoming they are. This is the latest creator clarification and supersedes any previous ambiguous claim that Ogres are simply undistinguished from other commonplace western peoples or that Goblins are the only people subjected to fear or prejudice. Neither category has fixed moral alignment, and the existing sixfold population model is unchanged. ## Earlier western social interpretation — superseded where clarified above Latest creator clarification, overriding the immediately preceding broad interpretation: Both Goblins and Ogres are common, ordinary inhabitants of western Avarra, with permanent families, villages, market districts, industries, travelling households, and all sorts of jobs and social positions. Goblins specifically experience substantial, widespread discrimination in western society. This may manifest through racist folklore, exclusionary local guilds and schools, unequal trade terms, suspicious guards, restricted civic rights or property tenure, segregated neighborhoods, hostile villages and habitual stereotyping, with actual severity varying across kingdoms, courts, regions and individual communities. Some cities recognize full equal citizenship and some Goblin institutions are powerful and independent; persistent discrimination remains an important feature of the wider western social reality. A Goblin individual's morality, honesty, intellect or occupation is not determined by those prejudices. Do not transfer Goblin-specific thieving/conniving stereotypes to Ogres: Ogres are instead widely feared for their strength and perceived dangerousness, not presumed schemers. Ogres are equally legitimate and often encountered western residents, and their size may have practical or local social consequences, but the creator's 'heavily discriminated' statement was expressly about Goblins. No uniform Ogre persecution statute is established, but fear may produce varying levels of suspicion, avoidance and discrimination. Ogres may be craftsmen, scholars, soldiers, officials, farmers, haulers, parents, wanderers, merchants or outlaws as individuals, with diverse social experiences. Neither people is a comic prop, innately evil, politically unified or required to live only in western lands. Avarra's already modeled population totals are redistributed socially and regionally without adding extra individuals or changing birth rates. ## Goblins — commerce, mutual aid, craft and wildly different politics | Subculture | Location and locally admired paths | Problems and disagreements | | --- | --- | --- | | Ironrill Burrow Councils | Ironspine valleys and mining towns: ventilation, council service, tunnel farming, safe extraction | Kin-based leasing systems can favor elders over young tradespeople | | Shattered Coast Street Guilds | Orrisport, Nine-Tin Bells and island ports: brokerage, dockcraft, legal wit, multilingual networks | Wealthy brokers versus dockworkers; smuggling is a factional crime, not racial destiny | | Eastern Well-Keepers | Avarran/Orundel caravan settlements: road knowledge, cistern repair, water arbitration | Toll wars and pressures from strong clans or armies | | North-Frost Hearths | Tharvorn's Iceburrow settlements: communal heat, winter preparation, ice-road craft | Adults quarrel over fuel rationing and public versus private storage | | Free Lantern Goblins | Cosmopolitan towns everywhere: schools, theatres, cooperative banks, civic reform | Criticize distant clan customs, and conservative kin may dismiss them | Reputation and variation: Some outside cultures associate Goblins with trickery or theft; that is a rumor, sometimes traceable to actual criminal bands, never a mandatory trait. A Goblin mayor may champion strict public weights; a Goblin mercenary may be dangerously corrupt. Large family groups and chosen guild households both possible. ## Ents — grove politics and multi-century commitments | Subculture | Locality and purpose | Internal dispute | | --- | --- | --- | | Letharion Rootwardens | Western Avarra ancient forests: long grove stewardship and negotiated access | Younger groves favor diplomacy, older guardians insist on strict exclusion | | Vaelora Elderwood Assemblies | Western continent ancient canopies: protecting watersheds and forest succession | Divisions over helping towns versus limiting contact | | Tharvorn Deep-Fir Keepers | Old boreal stands: winter resilience and careful fire management | Risk of remaining immobile while climate and neighbors change | | Orundel Rainward Groves | Humid forests: riverbank integrity, species diversity and intergenerational memory | Dilemmas when flood-control canals affect tree roots | Not copied Khazari values: Their respectable life need not be judged by paid work or craft mastery. Patience, stewardship and protective action may matter more; even within groves the speed and meaning of care are disputed. Ent kinship/reproduction remain unspecified unless previously established; don't invent Ent children or reproductive cycles. ## Centaurs — pasture is only one form of freedom | Subculture | Home and esteemed choices | Social tension | | --- | --- | --- | | Seven Wells Grazing Circles | Avarran eastern steppe: honorable pasture sharing, caring for herds, mobile leadership | Enclosure by city farms; conflict over water | | Orundel Open-Sky Houses | Great eastern grasslands: athletic skill, storytelling, scouting, medicine, astronomy | Clan autonomy versus confederation treaties | | Tharvorn Winter-Movers | Northern steppe: food storage, harsh-weather migrations, collective decisions | Disputes over season routes and staying near towns | | City-Gate Centaurs | Major mixed cities: urban physicians, scribes, couriers, civil judges | Accessibility, stable-yard stereotypes and limits on mobility | | Free Reed Pedagogues | Sahrad savanna routes: oral teaching, dispute mediation, stewardship of seasonal wells | Elders resist novel settlement agreements | Family and worth: Mobile bands may have robust multi-household relatives, foster children and allied clans, but a settled urban Centaur is not automatically regarded as a failure. Dissent concerns freedom and responsibility, not a universal need to travel. ## Merfolk — undersea sovereignty is varied | Subculture | Region and respected roles | Conflict | | --- | --- | --- | | Blue Shell Treaty Houses | Shattered Isles shelves: diplomats, fisher stewards, coastal law keepers | Surface merchants may violate reef rights | | Sahradi Current Courts | Crown Sea and warmer deltas: estuary engineers, tidal gardeners, ocean scholars | Canal pollution and unequal port access | | Orundel Reef Navigators | Eastern ocean current routes: mapmakers, safety pilots, educators | Control of navigation secrets and tolls | | Vaelora Deepwater Cities | Western ocean shelves: coldwater cultivators, artistic shells, intercity messengers | Undersea boundaries and salvage conflicts | | Tharvorn Brine Keepers | Northern fjords: storm pilots, winter nursery keepers and ice-edge fishers | Hard survival sometimes makes isolationism attractive | Biology and household restraint: Merfolk kin and households can be extensive; no invented fertility rates or universal family architecture. Undersea cities are not dry human cities, and visiting surface markets needs actual tide basins, access and agreements. Calling them “household spirits” is an outsider's claim, not confirmed species biology. ## Magical concealment of fairy-tale settlements — worldwide creator rule (21 November 2026) Creator-established extension of the living fairy-tale world: A large number of communities, settlements, hamlets, islands, groves, cave networks and even sizable villages or towns of Eryndor's many established intelligent peoples may be hidden through magic. Concealment may work in concert with ordinary remoteness, woodland cover, wetlands, confusing terrain or political secrecy. This is a real and widespread option throughout the five continents and islands, not a single token magical village or a privilege reserved for one species. An Ogre swamp village or island, Pixie canopy settlement, Aelwyn court, Gnome or Goblin hill community, Mushroom-folk cavern network and other fairy-tale settlements may be partly or wholly unknown even to nearby outsiders. Entire populated enclaves can exist among otherwise surveyed landscapes. Not an automatic species trait: Many Ogres, Goblins, Pixies, Fae, Gnomes and other folk also live openly in public villages, mixed markets, ports, cities and rural districts. Do not make every settlement magical, invisible, isolated, safe or inaccessible. Magical concealment need not be permanent, perfect, universal or the same everywhere. Some people can know a hidden settlement and trade with it; inhabitants can leave and visit outsiders; concealment can be incomplete, fallible, selective, locally maintained, or occasionally overcome, but no exact mechanism, bypass, moon assignment or failure rule is canonized merely by this principle. Even when hidden, settlements require viable food/water, internal social relations, waste disposal, crafts and trade according to local ecology. Magic consistency and geographic mystery: The moons are real sources of lunar magic; people know that but not which moon governs which effect or how lunar magic works. The planet independently generates Natural Magic, and individual peoples maintain their already established traditions (Khazari Runecraft/Deepcraft, Eldar, Aelwyn Fae, Pixie/fairy, Gnome, etc.). Concealment may be produced by suitable magic but is not automatically a new universal discipline or explained by one known moon, divine force or prayer. The Veiled Inland Sea is already an unusual hidden region: its established external inaccessibility and interior shore community network remain, but its precise concealment mechanism is separately unresolved and must not be copied onto all hidden villages. Atlas and campaign safeguards: Regional maps can depict known hidden communities on private informed charts with appropriate uncertainty, while public maps may omit them or record conflicting rumors. Do not populate all blank areas with named settlements or announce secrets to characters without discovery. Preserve the creator's 6× modeled world population without double counting residents of hidden communities and leave uncensused enclaves truly uncertain. Gloin's campaign remains paused at Autumn Day 22, Year 3847 of the Era of Crowns, Fifth Age, approximately 11:25 AM; the character has no new automatic knowledge of any secret location. ## Worldwide fairy-tale peoples — full communities and classic folklore lifestyles coexist (creator rule, 21 November 2026) Creator's explicit generalization of the Ogre rule: Throughout all of Eryndor, across all five continents and islands, the established fairy-tale and whimsical peoples should occur both in their recognizable folkloric settings AND in completely developed villages, town districts, island settlements, societies and mixed urban communities. A few individuals or a single token village are not sufficient. There can be whole settlements populated predominantly by the same people, as well as mixed-species market towns and independent families. These are normal lived places, with children, elders, occupations, neighbors, law, trade, festivities, histories, economies and disagreements. The specific Ogre precedent is real: some live in lone swamp huts, others form sizable Ogre swamp villages, island communities or marshland clans, and still others live in cities or unrelated climates. Never impose that archetypal lifestyle on every member of a people. Broader application as illustrative environmental/cultural possibilities (not rigid habitat assignments): Some Goblins may maintain burrow hamlets, crowded trading quarters, road camps or market towns; some Pixies may occupy full treetop or garden settlements rather than solitary flowers; some Brownies/Boggarts may maintain farm-edge hamlets, old manor quarters or hedgerow communities; some Trolls may inhabit bridge-side family settlements, marsh villages or highland communities; some Satyrs/Fauns may form orchard/woodland communities; some Gnomes may have villages, learned workshops or river towns; some Mushroom folk may inhabit damp forest floor or cavern settlements; some Harpies may have cliffside towns or roost communities; some Minotaurs may build broad-street towns or agricultural centers. Apply the same principle to other established folklore-like peoples (Kobolds, Halflings, Giants, Centaurs, animal-featured peoples, Merfolk, etc.) where their actual biology, terrain and societies allow. Not every example must appear in every region. The creator may later change or reject particular examples without invalidating the general rule. Tone and social variation: Preserve the classic fairy-tale charm, danger, strangeness, myth and occasional dark menace. Some hermits and enclaves really are frightening, hostile, predatory, magical or unusual; others are welcoming or ordinary, and settlements have internal differences. No sapient people is uniformly sweet, stupid, murderous, comical, primitive, isolated or predetermined morally good/evil by ancestry. Modern cultural and political realities, including western fear of Ogres and distrust/discrimination against Goblins rooted in eastern–western wars, continue to exist alongside these real communities. Civilizations can include both long-established regional homelands and diaspora/mixed towns. Map and simulation guardrails: New atlas maps should show clusters and networks of villages, island towns, marsh communities, woodland boroughs and distinctive local settlements across the vast expanse rather than isolated one-off folklore pins. Their places must have food, water, exchange, transport, protection and geography appropriate to scale. Do not invent exact population counts, rulers, species-specific fertility, additional moons, universal magical powers or a new kingdom merely from an illustration. The current sixfold population model is redistributed rather than inflated. Avarra's seven Throne mountain ring/Veiled Inland Sea, the vast Letharion forest, two different western human culture belts, eastern Urakai badlands and very rare/unsettled Eastern Grasslands Urakai remain as most recently corrected. This creator-level worldbuilding doesn't advance Gloin's campaign. ## Some Ogres live as classic fairy-tale swamp and woodland hermits — not all (creator clarification, 21 November 2026) Explicit limit: Preserve the classic fairy-tale Ogre as one real and recurring kind of Ogre lifestyle, not a universal Ogre species trait. Some Ogres live in secluded swamp huts, lonely marsh or forest-edge cottages, bog islands, old clearings or rough timber-and-stone dwellings. A solitary Ogre's home might have a smoking chimney, oversized cooking pot, vegetable patch, fishing traps, muddy paths and old warnings from neighboring villages. Some such Ogres are dangerous, frightening, unfriendly or predatory; others are quiet, eccentric, hospitable, misunderstood, or simply want to live alone. Avoid deciding the temperament of any particular hermit before a story establishes it. Most importantly, do NOT make all Ogres solitary swamp monsters. Many other Ogres have spouses and extended families, farms, town homes, organized hamlets and cities, businesses, courts, crafts, scholarship, military roles, mixed-species neighborhoods and varied religious life. Some live in forests, cities, highlands, riversides or the southeastern badlands. The creator's previously established cultural diversity, economic realism and longstanding families apply without exception. Western Ogres are commonly encountered but generally feared because of old eastern-war associations and reputation for strength, while Goblins are commonly encountered but distrusted under stereotypes of theft and scheming. Neither stereotype describes every person. Continuity: These fairy-tale hamlets and swamp huts add texture to the huge settled western continent without automatically naming a new location, assigning an Ogre personality, multiplying population, connecting anyone to Gloin's ancestry, or advancing the paused campaign. An artist may place a few Ogre huts in the marshland and some Ogre civic settlements in surrounding town country; do not cover every wetland with them or portray an Ogre hut as the mandatory default for Ogre society. ## Ogres — family, strength, scholarship, and the possibility of violence | Subculture | Locale and respected ways | Conflict | | --- | --- | --- | | River Carrying Families | Avarran/Orundel river towns: lifting, ferry upkeep, safe heavy transport | Gangs may exploit porters; safety versus low-cost contracts | | Ironspine Cliff Kin | Highland hamlets: guarding family passes, large-scale masonry | Remote clans sometimes feud over narrow routes | | Candleburrow Hearths | Tharvorn sheltered valleys: winter food stores, extended kin aid | Winter scarcity, suspicion from outsiders | | Red Mesa Wanderers | Sahradi plateaus: seasonal camps, stone craft and guest protocols | Water conflicts and violent raiding groups | | Mixed-Town Gentle Trades | Bramblebridge, urban docks, foreign towns: carpentry, medicine, poetry or engineering | Some locals unfairly expect all Ogres to be guards | Rule: An Ogre who has lived peacefully for years can commit an appalling act, and another may dedicate a lifetime to care.
